summary: - Use everyday, body‑related mysteries (eyes, onions, leg numbness) as topics because they consistently keep viewers past the first seconds. - Write hooks in second‑person, stating a surprising claim about the viewer’s own experience (e.g., “Your eyes are leaking right now…”). - Keep titles under eight words, start with “Why” or a direct question, and add a single emoji for visual punch. - Limit video length to 15‑20 seconds for optimal stay‑through; avoid exceeding 30 seconds unless the hook is exceptionally strong. - Drop generic countdown timers or overly technical intros that don’t immediately promise a personal revelation.
winning_hooks: Your eyes are leaking right now, and your brain is hiding it.
You are not sad when you chop an onion – it’s something else.
Your leg doesn’t actually fall asleep because of blood loss.
avoid: Opening with a generic “Did you know…”, long pre‑amble before the hook, countdown timers that delay the core claim, titles longer than eight words without a clear curiosity trigger
next_experiment: Create two versions of the same video: Version A uses a second‑person hook (“Your X is doing Y”) and Version B uses a third‑person hook (“People think X does Y”). Keep title, length, and thumbnail identical, then compare stayed_pct to see which phrasing drives higher retention.
